item.problem_statement: Death, treatment discontinuation and competing clinical events change what an outcome contrast means. ICH E9(R1) requires that intercurrent events be handled explicitly, and the causal competing-risks literature distinguishes total effects, controlled direct effects and separable effects, each answering a different question. Applied emulations default to cause-specific hazards or to censoring at the competing event. Censoring does not select among those estimands: it alters the observed-data analysis, and it corresponds to a hypothetical elimination of the competing event only when that intervention is well defined and its identification conditions hold, which is a claim the analysis has to make and defend. item.paper: A generalized theory of separable effects in competing event settings.
item.evidence: The registry entry says death and other intercurrent events are handled as data cleaning rather than as an identifying choice. This supplies the missing apparatus for one route: a formally defined estimand, identification conditions weak enough to allow time-varying common causes of the outcome, the competing event and censoring, implementable weighted estimators, and named sensitivity analyses. It also states plainly why the two standard alternatives fail, controlled direct effects requiring an intervention nobody can implement and natural effects resting on cross-world assumptions. What remains is availability: the conditions are still hard to meet with the data most studies hold.
item.quote: Even under our generalized conditions, the separable effects may be difficult to identify given currently available data in many studies.

verdicts.reason: The quote concerns whether separable effects may be empirically scrutinized in future studies. It neither proposes a reporting panel nor establishes a general distinction between which assumptions in an emulation are diagnostically interrogable and which are not.

item.problem_title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
item.problem_statement: Exchangeability and consistency cannot be established from observed data. Neither, strictly, can positivity, model correctness or phenotype validity: the available checks reveal or falsify particular problems and certify none of them. Current reports blur both distinctions. A propensity-score overlap plot is offered and the reader infers that the assumptions have been checked, when the plot is a partial diagnostic of one of them and silent on the rest. No standard panel exists, so what appears varies by author and by journal, and an absent diagnostic cannot be distinguished from one that was run and not reported. A single panel cannot be adequate for every design, which is a constraint on the solution rather than an argument against it.
item.paper: A generalized theory of separable effects in competing event settings.
item.evidence: The registry entry asks for a distinction between assumptions that can be interrogated and assumptions that cannot. Separable effects are constructed so that the reasoning behind them is falsifiable in a subsequent trial, in explicit contrast to natural effects, whose identifying assumptions are untestable even in principle. That is a worked example of moving an assumption across the diagnosable boundary rather than a dashboard for reporting the whole set.
item.quote: We stress that unlike previous definitions of direct and indirect effects, the separable effects can be subject to empirical scrutiny in future studies.

verdicts.reason: The paper provides a constructive simulation framework in which the causal data-generating mechanism and fitted model forms are known, which is relevant to causal estimator benchmarking. Its scope is narrow and does not validate broad generative patient models or permit causal claims from synthetic data lacking causal assumptions.

item.problem_title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
item.problem_statement: Generative patient models would support privacy-preserving code development, power planning and method stress testing, and synthetic patient data have shown value as a benchmark environment. The evaluation does not match the use. Marginal and temporal fidelity do not validate a generator's counterfactual behavior, and cannot: without identifying assumptions or interventional ground truth, two generators indistinguishable on observed data can disagree on some interventions. A model optimized for fidelity can therefore reproduce every observed association while generating wrong counterfactuals, wrong overlap and wrong time ordering, because none of those appears in the loss. Privacy mechanisms compound it by suppressing rare patterns, which are often the causally important ones. item.paper: Simulating longitudinal data from marginal structural models using the additive hazard model.
item.evidence: The registry entry says synthetic data are judged on distributional fidelity and then used for causal work. This supplies the criterion that matters instead: congeniality between the generating mechanism and the causal model to be fitted, derived rather than assumed. A simulation built this way is a valid benchmark for a causal estimator regardless of how realistic its marginals look. The scope is a marginal structural model for a time-to-event outcome, so the criterion does not yet cover generative patient models more broadly.
item.quote: In a simulation, it is important to be able to generate the data in such a way that the correct forms of any models to be fitted to those data are known.

verdicts.reason: The paper supports better-designed method comparisons and correctly identifies flaws in some existing comparisons. That is useful infrastructure, but it does not answer the registry's central question of defensibly selecting an estimator in an applied emulation or requiring robustness across choices.

item.problem_title: No estimator is defensible as a default, and no study is required to show that its choice mattered
item.problem_statement: The available estimators differ in what they assume rather than only in how they perform. Active-comparator new-user designs with regression or propensity adjustment handle baseline initiation and not treatment-confounder feedback. Matching gives a transparent population, discards information, and often leaves its estimand unstated. Marginal structural models represent regime effects directly and are unstable under extreme weights. The parametric g-formula supports flexible estimands and is sensitive to sequential outcome-model misspecification. G-estimation avoids modeling the treatment-free outcome distribution and is technically demanding. Longitudinal targeted learning is doubly robust, computationally heavy and sensitive to practical positivity. item.evidence: Comparing estimators requires a data-generating mechanism under which each competing model is correctly specified, and the paper supplies the derivation that makes such a comparison constructible. It also records that comparisons of causal methods are rare and that at least one published comparison was invalid, having contrasted a marginal estimand with a conditional one under a mechanism that made neither model correct. item.problem_title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
item.problem_statement: An internally valid estimate need not apply to the health system, population or calendar period where the decision will be made. Transporting an observational contrast requires treatment exchangeability in the source, effect exchangeability across samples conditional on a sufficient measured set, and positivity for both treatment and sampling. A sufficient set is weaker than every effect modifier: modifiers that do not differ across populations or that are irrelevant after conditioning need not be observed. Transport estimators are now being applied to emulations, including post hoc standardization of emulations to their trial populations inside a benchmarking program. What remains is the accounting. This is the accounting, for the trial-to-target case: a table of which potential outcome means and which participation probabilities are identifiable under each sampling scheme, with the non-nested design shown to lose the marginal target-population mean outright. item.problem_statement: Biomarkers and diagnoses are observed when a patient attends care and a clinician orders a test. item.paper: Doubly robust estimator of risk in the presence of censoring dependent on time-varying covariates: application to a primary prevention trial for coronary events with pravastatin.
item.evidence: The registry entry says the observation and censoring process is treated as a nuisance to be imputed. Here it is modeled as a hazard that depends on time-varying covariates and is given double protection against misspecification, which is more than imputation under a fixed missingness assumption. The limit is stated plainly: if censoring and event time remain dependent after conditioning on measured covariates, which is the case the entry is about since the visit process tracks latent severity, this estimator and every existing one fail.
item.quote: However, in a situation that censoring and event time are not independent even if we condition on time-varying covariates, our proposed estimator and other existing estimators cannot correct for selection bias.

It does not address continuous-time filtration-based identification, within-interval effects, or treatment-dependent observation, which define the registered problem.

item.problem_title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
item.problem_statement: Treatments, outcomes and clinical observations occur asynchronously and are recorded at times determined by the care process. Discretizing that onto a grid can reverse the temporal ordering of a treatment and an outcome falling in the same interval, merge several events into one, and define an estimand that exists only relative to the chosen interval.
